why.correct: Atoms bond into molecules; molecules are arranged into cells; similar cells group into tissues; two or more tissues build an organ; organs that share a job form an organ system; and all the organ systems together make the organism. Each level is built from the one below it.
Between the cell and the organ sits the tissue: a group of similar cells, with the material around them, working on one job. Organs are built from two or more kinds of tissue.
options: Molecules belong to the chemical level, which comes before the cell. The gap sits after the cell, so it must be something built from cells.
Correct. Similar cells group into tissues, and two or more kinds of tissue make an organ.
The organism is the top level, a whole living individual. It is already at the end of the sequence.
An organ system is a group of organs, so it comes after the organ, not before it. It already appears later in the sequence.

why.correct: Anatomy (ana- = apart, -tomy = cutting) is the study of structure: shape, parts and position. Physiology (physi/o = nature, -logy = study of) is the study of how structures work, the chemical and physical events inside them.
options: Correct. Structure versus function is the dividing line, and the two are linked because function follows from structure.
Both subjects work at every scale. Microscopic anatomy studies cells, and physiology studies whole organs such as the heart. Scale is not what separates them.
Both subjects study healthy bodies first. The study of disease is a different field, pathology.
Systemic anatomy studies one system at a time, and physiology studies whole-body events too. Whole versus part does not separate the two subjects.

why.correct: Measuring how fast chambers fill is studying how the heart works, an event over time. That is physiology.
options: Gross anatomy would describe the size, shape and position of the heart's chambers, not how fast they fill.
Microscopic anatomy would look at heart cells and tissue under a microscope. Filling speed is a working event, not a structure.
Correct. Physiology studies how structures work, and a filling rate is a measure of function.
Regional anatomy studies all the structures in one body part together, such as the chest. It describes structure, not the speed of an event.

why.correct: Studying every structure in one part of the body together is regional anatomy. Surgeons work this way because an operation happens in one region, where all the systems overlap.
options: Systemic anatomy follows one system through the whole body, for example every bone. The surgeon is doing the opposite: every system in one place.
Microscopic anatomy needs a microscope. The hand's bones, muscles and vessels are gross structures.
Physiology studies how structures work. The surgeon is reviewing structure and position.
Correct. One region, every structure in it, is regional anatomy.

why.correct: The bladder is built from two or more kinds of tissue, has a recognizable shape and does a specific job (storing urine). That is the definition of an organ.
options: A tissue is one group of similar cells. The bladder contains several kinds of tissue, so it is a level above tissue.
Correct. Several tissues combined into one structure with one job make an organ.
The organ system is the urinary system: kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra together. The bladder alone is one of its organs.
A cell is a single unit. The bladder is made of millions of cells arranged in tissues.

why.correct: The digestive system includes the tube food passes through (mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, with the appendix attached) and the organs that feed juices into it (liver, gallbladder, pancreas).
options: Correct. The liver makes bile, a digestive juice that helps digest fatty foods, so it belongs to the digestive system.
The spleen sits near the stomach but belongs to the lymphatic system. It filters blood and houses immune cells.
Correct. The gallbladder stores bile from the liver and releases it into the intestine.
Correct. The esophagus carries food from the throat to the stomach.
The kidney belongs to the urinary system. It filters blood and makes urine.
Correct. The appendix is a small pouch attached to the intestine, so it is part of the digestive system.

why.correct: The pancreas and the gonads (testes and ovaries) each belong to two systems. Each releases hormones into the blood (endocrine system) and also does a second job.
options: Correct. The pancreas releases digestive juices into the intestine (digestive system) and hormones into the blood (endocrine system).
Correct. A testis makes sperm cells (reproductive system) and releases hormones into the blood (endocrine system).
The urinary bladder stores urine until you empty it. It is an organ of the urinary system only.
Correct. An ovary releases egg cells (reproductive system) and hormones into the blood (endocrine system).
The trachea is the airway to the lungs, an organ of the respiratory system only.

why.correct: Vessels are named by the direction of flow relative to the heart. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content.
options: Most arteries do carry blood high in oxygen, but not all. The arteries from the heart to the lungs carry blood low in oxygen and are still arteries.
Correct. Away from the heart defines an artery.
A wall one cell thick describes a capillary. Arteries have thick, muscular walls.
Carrying blood back to the heart defines a vein.

why.correct: Capillaries have a wall only one layer of flat cells thick, so oxygen, nutrients and wastes can pass across it. Thicker vessel walls do not allow much exchange.
options: Arteries carry blood toward the tissues, but their walls are thick and muscular. Little oxygen crosses them.
Veins carry blood back toward the heart after exchange has already happened in the capillaries.
Correct. The thin capillary wall is the structure that allows exchange: structure sets function.
Blood in the heart's chambers does not supply the cells of the calf. The heart pumps blood out to the vessels that reach the calf.

why.correct: Responsiveness is the ability to detect a change (heat on the skin) and react to it (moving the hand).
options: Growth is an increase in size. Nothing grows when you pull your hand away.
Reproduction is making new cells or a new organism. It plays no part in this reaction.
Metabolism is the sum of the body's chemical changes. It powers the muscles, but the event described is detecting a change and reacting.
Correct. Detect a change, react to it: that is responsiveness.

why.correct: Metabolism (meta- = change, bol = throw) is every chemical change in your body: building large molecules from small ones, which uses energy, and breaking large molecules down, which releases energy.
options: Correct. Metabolism covers both building up and breaking down, in every cell.
Breaking food down in the stomach is digestion, one small part of the body's chemical activity.
Heart rate is one measure of cardiovascular function, not the definition of metabolism.
More cells means growth. Metabolism supplies the energy and materials for growth, but it is not the same thing.

why.correct: The order is reversed in that step. Similar cells group into tissues, and two or more kinds of tissue build an organ. Organs never combine to make a tissue.
options: This step is right. Atoms bond to form molecules, such as water.
This step is right. Molecules arranged in the right way make a cell.
This is the wrong step. Tissues build organs, not the other way round.
This step is right. The stomach, intestines and liver, for example, form the digestive system.
This step is right. All the organ systems together make a whole living individual.

why.correct: A change (cooling) is detected and triggers a response (heat from shivering) that pushes temperature back. The result is a value held within a normal range. The feedback loop topic later in Foundations shows the full mechanism.
options: Body temperature does change, which is why the response is triggered. It is kept within a range, not fixed at one value.
Correct. Detecting a change and pushing the value back keeps it within its normal range.
Muscles work in every temperature. Shivering is one response among the many things muscles do.
If the outside temperature set body temperature, you would cool along with the air. The scenario shows the opposite.

why.correct: Higher up, less air presses down, so air pressure falls and each breath pushes less oxygen into your blood. Your organs and systems stay the same; only their oxygen supply changes.

variables.name: Pressure of the air around you
variables.why: Higher up, there is less air above you pressing down, so air pressure falls.

variables.name: Oxygen entering your blood with each breath
variables.why: Air pressure pushes oxygen into your blood. Lower air pressure pushes less oxygen in with each breath.

variables.name: Number of organ systems in your body
variables.why: Your organs and systems stay the same. What changes is how well they are supplied with oxygen.

why.correct: The kidneys normally remove extra water from the blood. When they fail, water builds up, some collects in the lungs, less oxygen can enter the blood, and he feels short of breath. One system's failure changes conditions for another.
options: Correct. The urinary problem reaches the respiratory system through the extra fluid carried by the cardiovascular system.
The kidneys do not act on the airway directly. The link is the fluid that builds up in the blood.
The scenario begins with the kidneys. The lung problem follows from their failure, not the reverse.
Ankle swelling and lung fluid are both results of the same water buildup. The ankles cannot press on the lungs.

why.correct: The thymus and the spleen are lymphatic organs. The lymphatic system returns leaked fluid to the blood and houses immune cells.
options: The thymus does release a few hormones into the blood, but both the thymus and the spleen are classed as lymphatic organs. The endocrine system's main organs are the pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas and gonads.
The spleen sits next to the stomach, but it is not part of the digestive tube and makes no digestive juice.
The spleen filters blood, but it is classed with the lymphatic organs, not with the heart and vessels.
Correct. Thymus and spleen are lymphatic organs.

why.correct: The single urethra drains the bladder to the outside. The two ureters bring urine into the bladder from the kidneys.
options: The ureters carry urine from each kidney down to the bladder, into it rather than out of it.
Correct. The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
A uterine tube carries an egg cell from an ovary to the uterus. It is a reproductive organ.
The kidneys make urine. They do not carry it out of the body.

why.correct: The word root carries the core meaning. In gastritis that is gastr, "stomach". The ending -itis adds "inflamed".
options: Correct. gastr is the root; it names the body part, the stomach.
-itis is a suffix. It sits at the end and says the term names a condition: something inflamed.
gastr/o is the combining form, the root plus a linking vowel. In gastritis the vowel is dropped because -itis starts with a vowel, so the root alone is present.
Gastritis contains no combining vowel. It is dropped before a suffix that begins with a vowel.

why.correct: A combining form is a root with its combining vowel, almost always o, written with a slash: cardi/o, gastr/o, hepat/o. The vowel makes the parts easy to join and say.
options: A term with only a prefix and a suffix, such as tachypnea, exists, but it is not what "combining form" means.
Roots joined to each other keep a vowel between them, as in gastroenterology. Joining them without one is the opposite of a combining form.
Correct. Root plus combining vowel is a combining form.
Suffixes such as -ac and -al do make adjectives, but they are suffixes, not combining forms.

why.correct: Read the suffix first: -megaly means enlargement. The root hepat means liver. Hepatomegaly is an enlarged liver.
options: Pain would be the suffix -algia. The term here ends in -megaly.
Correct. hepat (liver) + o + megaly (enlargement).
Removal would be the suffix -ectomy, as in hepatectomy.
Inflamed would be the suffix -itis. The term here ends in -megaly.

why.correct: -ectomy means cutting out (ec- = out, tom = cut). Nephrectomy is removal of a kidney.
options: -tomy means cutting into. A nephrotomy is an incision into the kidney; the kidney stays.
-ostomy means making an opening. A nephrostomy is a tube opening from the kidney through the skin; the kidney stays.
-logy means study of. Nephrology is the medical field that studies the kidneys.
Correct. nephr (kidney) + ectomy (cutting out).

why.correct: The prefix brady- means slow and -pnea means breathing. Bradypnea is slow breathing.
options: Correct. brady- (slow) + -pnea (breathing).
tachy- means fast. Tachypnea is fast breathing, the opposite of this patient.
a- means without. Apnea means no breathing at all, and this patient is breathing.
dys- means difficult. Dyspnea describes breathing that feels hard, whatever its rate.

why.correct: A prefix sits before the root. sub- (under), peri- (around) and inter- (between) are prefixes. The other terms start directly with a root.
options: Correct. sub- (under) + cutane (skin) + -ous (pertaining to).
Cardiology is cardi (root) + o + logy (suffix). It starts with the root.
Correct. peri- (around) + card (heart) + -itis (inflamed).
Gastritis is gastr (root) + itis (suffix). It starts with the root.
Correct. inter- (between) + cost (rib) + -al (pertaining to).
Hepatomegaly is hepat (root) + o + megaly (suffix). It starts with the root.

why.correct: Suffix first, because it says what kind of word you have (condition, procedure, field). Then the prefix, then the roots. Combine starting from the suffix, and finally confirm the meaning, because literal meanings are sometimes off.
The combining vowel is dropped before a suffix that begins with a vowel. -itis begins with i, so gastr/o + itis = gastritis.
options: Keeping the o before a vowel breaks the rule and makes an awkward double vowel.
Correct. Drop the o before a suffix starting with a vowel.
This keeps the o and adds an extra t between the parts. Neither belongs: the o is dropped, and the suffix is simply -itis.
This keeps the o and shortens the suffix to -tis. The suffix stays whole as -itis; it is the o that gets dropped.

why.correct: Between two roots the combining vowel stays, even when the next root starts with a vowel. So gastr + o + enter + o + logy = gastroenterology.
options: Correct. The combining vowel o is kept between roots.
Dropping the vowel happens only before a suffix that starts with a vowel. Here the next part is a root, so the vowel stays.
The combining vowel is almost always o. "Gastraenterology" is not a term.
The combining vowel is almost always o. "Gastrienterology" is not a term.

why.correct: The rule runs the other way: the combining vowel is dropped before a suffix that begins with a vowel. Keeping it would give "gastroitis" instead of gastritis.
options: This step is right. gastr is the root for stomach.
This step is right. -itis means inflamed.
This is the wrong step. Before a suffix that starts with a vowel, the o is dropped.
This step is right. The parts are written as one word: gastritis.

why.correct: dys- means difficult or painful, and -uria means a condition of the urine. Dysuria is painful or difficult passing of urine, which is what she describes.
options: Correct. dys- (painful) + -uria (condition of the urine).
-ectomy is a procedure, removal. A cystectomy is removal of the bladder, not a symptom.
-logy names a field. Hematology is the study of blood, not a symptom.
-ostomy is a procedure that makes an opening. A nephrostomy drains the kidney through the skin.

why.correct: Many organs have a Latin root and a Greek root. ren is Latin and nephr is Greek, and both mean kidney. The Latin root often forms plain descriptive words (renal), while the Greek root often forms names of diseases and procedures (nephritis, nephrectomy).
options: Both roots mean the whole kidney. Neither is specific to one part of it.
Correct. Two languages, one organ: ren (Latin) and nephr (Greek).
The pattern runs roughly the other way: renal is a plain description, and nephr appears in many disease names. Neither root means healthy or diseased.
Both are roots. Each names the kidney itself; a prefix would only modify a root.

why.correct: -ectomy (cutting out), -scopy (looking inside with an instrument) and -plasty (surgical repair or reshaping) are things done to a patient. -algia, -megaly and -itis describe conditions a patient has.
options: Correct. -ectomy is removal, a procedure.
-algia means pain, a condition.
Correct. -scopy means looking inside with an instrument, as in arthroscopy.
-megaly means enlargement, a condition.
Correct. -plasty means surgical repair or reshaping, as in rhinoplasty.
-itis means inflamed, a condition.

why.correct: Root splen (spleen) + combining vowel o + suffix -megaly (enlargement). The vowel stays because -megaly starts with a consonant.
options: -ectomy means removal. A splenectomy removes the spleen.
-algia means pain. Splenalgia is pain in the spleen, not enlargement.
Correct. splen + o + megaly.
-itis means inflamed. Splenitis is an inflamed spleen, not an enlarged one.

why.correct: sub- means under, cutane means skin, and -ous means pertaining to. A subcutaneous injection goes just under the skin.
options: Into a vein is intravenous: intra- (inside) + ven (vein) + -ous.
Between one rib and the next is intercostal: inter- (between) + cost (rib) + -al.
Correct. sub- (under) + cutane (skin).
Into a muscle is intramuscular: intra- (inside) + muscul (muscle) + -ar.

why.correct: Ancient anatomists found arteries empty after death and guessed they carried air. The name kept that old guess. Word parts usually get you to the right meaning, but the definition is what counts.
options: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The air-duct name records an old mistake, not a fact.
Greek and Latin roots are equally useful. The problem here is an outdated idea behind the name, not the language.
Correct. Decoding gives the literal meaning; always confirm it with the definition.
Most terms can be decoded, with or without a prefix. Gastritis has no prefix and decodes cleanly.

why.correct: In the anatomical position the arms hang at the sides with the palms facing forward and the thumbs pointing away from the body.
options: Palms toward the thighs is how most people stand when relaxed, but it is not the anatomical position.
Correct. Palms forward, thumbs pointing away from the body.
Palms backward turns the thumbs toward the body, the opposite of the reference posture.
Palms toward the midline is the relaxed resting posture. The anatomical position turns the palms fully forward.

why.correct: Supine means lying face up, on the back. A handy link: supine, on your spine.
options: Prone means lying face down, the opposite of this patient.
Lateral is a directional term meaning away from the midline. It does not name a lying position.
Correct. Face up, on the back, is supine.
Caudal is a directional term meaning toward the tail end. It does not name a lying position.

why.correct: Medial (Latin medius = middle) means closer to the midline, the imaginary line dividing the body into equal right and left halves.
options: Lateral is the opposite: farther from the midline, toward the side.
Correct. Medial means toward the midline.
Proximal means nearer to where a limb attaches to the trunk, which is not the same as nearer the midline.
Superficial means toward the body surface, a different axis altogether.

why.correct: With the palms forward, the thumb points away from the body, so it lies farther from the midline than the little finger. The thumb is lateral.
options: The thumb is medial only if you picture the palms turned backward or in. In the anatomical position the palms face forward, so the little finger is the medial one.
Proximal and distal compare distance from the limb's attachment. The thumb and little finger are at about the same distance from the shoulder.
Deep compares distance from the surface. Both fingers are at the surface of the hand.
Correct. Palms forward puts the thumb on the lateral side.

why.correct: Proximal means nearer to where the limb attaches to the trunk. The elbow is nearer the shoulder than the wrist is, so the elbow is proximal to the wrist.
options: The wrist is farther from the shoulder than the elbow, so the wrist is distal to the elbow.
The ankle is farther from the hip than the knee, so the ankle is distal to the knee.
Correct. Elbow is nearer the attachment than the wrist.
The fingers are farther from the shoulder than the palm, so they are distal to it.

why.correct: The breastbone sits at the front of the chest, in front of the heart. Toward the front is anterior.
options: Correct. The breastbone is anterior to the heart.
Posterior means behind. The backbone, not the breastbone, is posterior to the heart.
The breastbone lies on the midline, directly in front of the heart. Neither is to the side of the other.
The breastbone runs along the front of the chest at the level of the heart, not below it.

why.correct: In an upright human, cranial matches superior, ventral matches anterior and dorsal matches posterior. Medial and lateral describe the midline, while proximal and distal describe distance along a limb, so those do not match.
options: Correct. Toward the head is both superior and cranial in a standing person.
Correct. The belly side of a human is the front.
Medial means toward the midline; proximal means nearer a limb's attachment. They are different axes.
Correct. The back of a human is both posterior and dorsal.
Lateral means away from the midline; distal means farther from a limb's attachment. They are different axes.

why.correct: From the surface inward, the thigh has skin, then fat, then muscle, then bone. Muscle lies farther from the surface than skin, so muscle is deep to the skin.
options: Bone is the innermost layer, so it is deep to muscle, not superficial to it.
The skin is the outermost layer, so it is superficial to the fat, not deep to it.
Correct. Muscle lies farther from the surface than skin.
The skin is at the surface and the bone is innermost, so the skin is superficial to the bone.

why.correct: Because most brain-body pathways cross the midline, damage on one side of the brain affects the opposite side of the body. The weakness is contralateral: the left arm and leg.
options: Weakness on the same side would be ipsilateral. That would happen only if the pathways stayed on one side, and most cross.
Correct. Right-sided brain damage, left-sided (contralateral) weakness.
Damage to one side of the brain affects one side of the body, not both legs.
The face on the same side would be ipsilateral, and the arm and leg would be spared. That does not fit crossing pathways.

why.correct: Ipsilateral (ipse = same, latus = side) means on the same side of the body.
options: Contralateral means on opposite sides, such as the right arm and left leg.
Bilateral means on both sides, as in both arms. It does not describe two structures on one side.
Intermediate means lying between a medial and a lateral structure.
Correct. Same side is ipsilateral.

why.correct: Directional terms always describe the body as if it stood in the anatomical position. Lying down changes nothing: the face is still anterior to the ears.
options: Superior means toward the head, not toward the ceiling. Her chest is still anterior.
Correct. Directional terms do not change when the body lies down.
Her feet are still inferior (and distal) to her knees. Lying down does not make them posterior.
Her back is still posterior to her chest. Inferior means toward the feet, not toward the mattress.

why.correct: Intermediate means lying between a more medial structure and a more lateral one. The eye lies between the nose and the ear.
options: Correct. Between medial and lateral is intermediate.
Proximal describes distance from a limb's attachment. The face is not on a limb.
Superficial compares distance from the surface, not position between two structures.
Contralateral means on the opposite side of the body. The eye, nose and ear here are on the same side.

why.correct: Proximal and distal measure distance along the limb from where it attaches to the trunk. The hand is farther from the shoulder than the elbow in every posture, so it is always distal to the elbow. Terms are also read from the anatomical position, not from a raised arm.
options: Correct. The hand is always distal to the elbow.
Bending the elbow does not change the order along the limb. The hand stays farther from the shoulder than the elbow, so it stays distal.
Proximal and distal are used mainly on the limbs, the opposite of this claim.
Lateral compares distance from the midline, which is not the student's mistake. The mistake is about proximal and distal.

why.correct: In the anatomical position the palms face forward and the thumbs point away from the body. Palms facing the thighs is the relaxed standing posture.
options: This item is right. Upright and facing forward is part of the reference posture.
This item is right. The feet are flat and point forward.
This item is right. The arms hang at the sides.
This is the wrong item. The palms face forward, not toward the thighs.

why.correct: Lateral on the forearm is the thumb side (palms forward). Left is the patient's left. Just proximal to the wrist means slightly toward the elbow from the wrist.
options: Correct. Thumb side, left arm, slightly toward the elbow from the wrist.
The little-finger side is medial, not lateral, and "just proximal to the wrist" is near the wrist, not the elbow.
The report says the left forearm, and the patient's left is meant. The back of the hand is distal to the wrist.
The little-finger side is medial, and toward the fingers from the wrist is distal, not proximal.

why.correct: Proximal means nearer the limb's attachment to the trunk, at the shoulder. Moving away from it you pass the elbow, the wrist, the palm and finally the fingertips, the most distal point.
Superficial means toward the body surface; its opposite is deep, away from the surface.
options: Correct. Superficial and deep are the pair.
Distal is the opposite of proximal.
Dorsal is the opposite of ventral.
Caudal is the opposite of cranial.

why.correct: The sagittal plane (sagitta = arrow) is a vertical plane running front to back, so it separates right from left.
options: The frontal plane runs side to side and separates anterior from posterior.
The transverse plane is horizontal and separates superior from inferior.
Correct. Sagittal planes divide right from left.
An oblique plane runs at a slant between the main planes, so it does not cleanly separate right from left.

why.correct: The frontal plane, also called the coronal plane, is a vertical plane running from side to side, so it separates front from back.
options: Correct. Frontal (coronal) planes divide anterior from posterior.
The midsagittal plane divides the body into equal right and left halves.
The transverse plane divides superior from inferior.
A parasagittal plane divides the body into unequal right and left parts.

why.correct: A vertical cut that stays on the right side, off the midline, is parasagittal. It divides the head into unequal right and left parts.
options: A midsagittal cut runs down the exact midline, through the middle of the nose.
A horizontal cut at eye level would pass through both eyes, not just the right one.
Correct. Off the midline, dividing right from left unequally: parasagittal.
A frontal cut through the eyes would pass through both eyes, since it runs from side to side.

why.correct: The frontal plane is also called the coronal plane (corona = crown), because it runs like a headband over the head from ear to ear.
options: The median plane is another name for the midsagittal plane.
Correct. Frontal and coronal name the same plane.
Horizontal is another name for the transverse plane.
Axial is the imaging name for the transverse plane.

why.correct: Cutting a tube straight across its length gives a ring: the wall around a hollow channel.
options: Correct. A tube cut across shows a ring.
A tube cut along its length shows two parallel walls with the channel between them, not a ring.
A solid ball cut through its middle gives a filled disk, with no hollow center.
A flat sheet cut at a slant gives a straight strip, not a closed ring.

why.correct: The transverse plane is also called the horizontal plane, imaging staff call it the axial plane, and the section it produces is a cross section.
options: Correct. Horizontal is another name for transverse.
Coronal is another name for the frontal plane.
Correct. A cut along the transverse plane is a cross section.
Correct. Axial is the imaging name for the transverse plane.
Median is another name for the midsagittal plane.

why.correct: A plane is an imaginary flat surface that sets a direction. A section is the actual surface you see once the body or an organ is divided along that plane.
options: Planes can be vertical (sagittal, frontal) or horizontal (transverse), and so can sections.
Correct. Plane = imaginary surface; section = the cut surface.
Both terms apply to organs and to the whole body.
Scans show sections too. CT, MRI and ultrasound all produce sections without any cutting.

why.correct: Ultrasound makes images from echoes of sound waves and uses no ionizing radiation. The gallbladder is a fluid-filled organ, which ultrasound shows well.
options: CT uses X-rays from many angles, a larger dose of ionizing radiation.
Correct. Sound waves, no ionizing radiation, and good views of fluid-filled organs.
PET uses a radioactive tracer, which exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
A radiograph uses X-rays, which are ionizing radiation.

why.correct: Dense bone absorbs more X-rays than soft tissue. Fewer rays reach the detector behind the bone, and those areas show as white.
options: Reflected sound waves are how ultrasound works, not radiographs.
Radio signals in a magnetic field are how MRI works.
Correct. More absorption means fewer X-rays reach the detector behind the bone, which shows as white.
Tracer uptake is how PET works. A radiograph uses no tracer.

why.correct: Beams pass through from many angles; detectors measure how much each is weakened; the computer turns those measurements into the density at each point; the densities become a grayscale transverse section; and a stack of sections can be rebuilt in other planes.

A radiograph is a shadow. Everything the beam crosses, front to back, is laid on top of everything else in one flat image, so depth is lost. A second view from the side, or a CT, shows which is in front.
options: Metal absorbs X-rays strongly, so a coin shows clearly as white. The problem is depth, not visibility.
Radiographs show bone and metal best of all. Soft tissue shows only as shades of gray.
X-rays pass through the heart; that is why its outline appears as a gray shadow rather than a solid block.
Correct. Projection, not section: depth is lost.

why.correct: Transverse CT images are viewed as if you stand at the patient's feet looking toward the head, just as when you face a person. The patient's right appears on the left of the screen. The liver lies on the patient's right.
options: The screen's left is the patient's right, the same as when you face someone.
The viewing convention is fixed, so the side can be read directly from the image.
Correct. Screen left is patient right.
The images are displayed in a standard orientation whatever the position of the patient in the scanner, so right and left still follow the convention.

why.correct: MRI uses a very strong magnet. It can pull on some metal objects in the body, so a metal fragment near the eye can move and cause injury.
options: A radiograph uses X-rays, which do not move metal. The fragment would simply show up white.
CT uses X-rays too. Metal causes bright streaks on the image but is not moved by the scan.
Ultrasound uses sound waves, which do not move metal fragments.
Correct. The MRI magnet is the hazard.

why.correct: PET uses an injected tracer that very active cells take up more of, so it maps activity. It is usually combined with CT to place that activity on the anatomy.
options: Correct. PET shows where cells are most active.
A radiograph shows density, mainly bone and air, not how active the cells are.
Ultrasound shows tissue boundaries and movement, not how active the cells are.
Dissection is done on a body after death and shows structure, not living activity.

why.correct: The transverse plane is horizontal, so it separates the upper (superior) part from the lower (inferior) part.
options: Medial and lateral compare distance from the midline; the sagittal plane divides along that direction.
Correct. Transverse separates superior from inferior.
Proximal and distal apply along a limb and are not divided by one standard plane.
Superficial and deep compare distance from the surface, not a direction a main plane divides.

why.correct: MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not X-rays or a tracer. The magnetic field lines up hydrogen nuclei, radio pulses disturb them, and their returning signals build the image.
options: This entry is right. Dense tissue absorbs more X-rays and appears white on the flat projection.
This entry is right. CT computes sections from many X-ray measurements.
This is the wrong entry. MRI uses a magnet and radio waves; a radioactive tracer belongs to PET.
This entry is right. Ultrasound builds a live section from echoes.

why.correct: The cranial cavity (crani/o = skull) is the space inside the skull, and it holds the brain. With the vertebral canal it forms the dorsal body cavity.
options: The vertebral canal is the other part of the dorsal body cavity. It runs down through the backbone and holds the spinal cord, not the brain.
The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity. It holds the heart, the trachea and the esophagus.
Correct. The brain sits in the cranial cavity, inside the skull.
The pericardial cavity is the thin fluid-filled space around the heart, in the mediastinum.

why.correct: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle that stretches across the trunk. Everything in the ventral body cavity above it is thoracic; everything below it is abdominopelvic.
options: Correct. The diaphragm is the muscular wall between the chest and the abdomen.
The mediastinum is the central region between the two lungs. It runs from the neck down to the diaphragm, but it does not divide the chest from the abdomen.
The pleura is the serous membrane around each lung. It stays above the diaphragm.
The peritoneum is the serous membrane of the abdominopelvic cavity. It lines the space below the diaphragm; it is not the wall between the two cavities.

why.correct: The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, between the lungs. It holds the heart, the large vessels, the trachea, the esophagus and the thymus.
options: Correct. The heart, wrapped in its own serous membrane, sits in the lower part of the mediastinum.
Each lung lies lateral to the mediastinum, wrapped by the pleura on its own side of the chest.
Correct. The esophagus runs down through the mediastinum, behind the trachea and heart.
Correct. The trachea (windpipe) runs down the mediastinum before it splits toward the lungs.
The spleen is below the diaphragm, in the abdominal cavity.
Correct. The thymus sits in the upper mediastinum, above the heart.

why.correct: The heart lies in the mediastinum, the central compartment between the two lungs, running from the breastbone in front to the backbone behind. A blade that reaches the heart has entered the mediastinum.
options: The left pleural cavity is the thin space around the left lung, lateral to the heart. The heart itself is in the mediastinum.
The abdominal cavity lies below the diaphragm. The heart is above it.
The vertebral canal is part of the dorsal body cavity, inside the backbone. It is posterior to the whole thoracic cavity.
Correct. The heart sits in the mediastinum, directly behind the breastbone.

why.correct: The parietal layer (paries = wall) lines the wall of the cavity. The membrane then folds back as the visceral layer to cover the organ.
options: The visceral layer (viscera = internal organs) covers the organ, not the wall.
Correct. Parietal means wall: it lines the cavity wall.
The serosa is the name often given to the visceral layer on the outside of an organ such as the stomach. It is on the organ, not the wall.
Serous fluid is the thin film between the two layers. It is not a layer of the membrane.

why.correct: The pleural cavity is only the thin, fluid-filled gap between the visceral layer on the lung and the parietal layer on the chest wall. The lung is covered by the visceral layer and lies outside that gap, like a fist in a balloon that never enters the air inside.
options: This is the common error. The organ is never inside its serous cavity; only a thin film of serous fluid is.
Correct. In the thoracic cavity, yes; in the pleural cavity, no.
The mediastinum is the central compartment between the lungs. The lungs lie lateral to it, and the pleural cavities surround the lungs, not lie below them.
Everything above the diaphragm is thoracic. The abdominopelvic cavity is below the diaphragm.

why.correct: The ventral body cavity contains the thoracic cavity above the diaphragm. The thoracic cavity contains the mediastinum between the lungs. The mediastinum contains the heart and the thin pericardial cavity around it.
The dorsal body cavity has two continuous parts: the cranial cavity inside the skull, holding the brain, and the vertebral canal inside the backbone, holding the spinal cord.
options: Correct. The vertebral canal is the lower part of the dorsal body cavity.
The pelvic cavity is the lower part of the abdominopelvic cavity, in the ventral body cavity.
The pleural cavities are serous spaces around the lungs, in the ventral body cavity.
The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, in the ventral body cavity.

why.correct: Normally a film of serous fluid lets the visceral layer on the lung glide over the parietal layer on the chest wall. When infection or injury makes the layers swollen and rough, they rub with each breath. The rubbing causes sharp pain and a grating sound.
options: The vertebral canal holds the spinal cord in the dorsal body cavity. It does not move with breathing and would not make a grating sound in the chest.
The lung and the pericardial cavity are on different sides of the mediastinum. The lung cannot slip into the heart's serous space.
Correct. Rough layers rub instead of gliding, and each breath moves them.
The diaphragm lies below the lungs. The mediastinum, not the diaphragm, separates the right and left pleural cavities, and that separation is normal.

why.correct: The peritoneum lines the abdominal wall (its parietal layer) and covers the abdominal organs (its visceral layer). To reach the stomach from the front, the surgeon cuts through the parietal layer into the peritoneal cavity.
options: The pleura surrounds the lungs, above the diaphragm. An incision in the front of the abdomen does not reach it.
The serous membrane around the heart is in the mediastinum, above the diaphragm.
Correct. The peritoneum lines the abdominopelvic cavity.
The brain's protective layers are in the dorsal body cavity, inside the skull.

why.correct: The urinary bladder lies in the pelvic cavity, the lower part of the abdominopelvic cavity, between your hip bones. When it fills, it rises into the abdominal cavity, because no wall separates the two.
options: Correct. The empty bladder sits low, in the pelvic cavity.
The thoracic cavity is above the diaphragm. It holds the heart and lungs.
The abdominal cavity is the upper part of the abdominopelvic cavity. A very full bladder can rise into it, but an empty one stays in the pelvis.
The vertebral canal is inside the backbone and holds the spinal cord.

why.correct: The layer lining the chest wall is the parietal layer (paries = wall). The needle crosses it and then reaches the fluid in the pleural cavity. The visceral layer is on the surface of the lung, beyond the fluid, and the needle should never reach it.
options: This step is right. The needle passes through the skin and fat first.
This step is right. Muscle forms much of the chest wall.
This is the wrong step. The needle crosses the parietal layer on the chest wall, not the visceral layer on the lung.
This step is right. The fluid collects in the pleural cavity, between the two layers.

why.correct: A serous cavity works because it is nearly empty. Fluid that fills it separates the layers and presses on the organ, so the heart cannot fill fully.

variables.name: Space between the two serous layers around the heart
variables.why: The extra fluid collects between the layers and pushes them apart.

variables.name: How fully the heart can fill between beats
variables.why: The fluid-filled sac presses on the heart from outside, so less blood can flow in to fill it.

variables.name: Number of layers in the serous membrane
variables.why: The membrane still has one parietal and one visceral layer; only the gap between them changes.

why.correct: The spleen lies in the abdominal cavity, covered by the peritoneum. Blood from its surface collects in the peritoneal cavity, between the layer on the organs and the layer lining the abdominal wall.
options: The left pleural cavity surrounds the left lung, above the diaphragm. The spleen is below it.
Correct. The spleen is an abdominal organ covered by peritoneum.
The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart, in the mediastinum.
The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, above the diaphragm.

why.correct: Two smooth, wet surfaces with a thin film of fluid between them slide past each other with very little friction. The heart beats and the lungs expand without the layers wearing.
options: Oxygen reaches organs in the blood. Serous fluid is a thin lubricating film.
Correct. The fluid film lets the visceral layer glide over the parietal layer.
The fluid is watery and thin. Protection from blows comes from bone and the body wall.
Serous fluid does not attach organs to bone. It lets them move.

why.correct: Below the diaphragm, the abdominal cavity holds the liver, spleen, stomach, intestines and, against its back wall, the kidneys. The pelvic cavity holds the urinary bladder.
options: Correct. The liver sits in the upper right of the abdominal cavity, just under the diaphragm.
The heart is in the mediastinum, above the diaphragm.
Correct. The bladder is in the pelvic cavity.
Correct. The kidneys lie against the back wall of the abdominal cavity, behind the peritoneum.
The thymus is in the upper mediastinum, above the heart.
Correct. The spleen is in the upper left of the abdominal cavity.

why.correct: Each lung has its own pleural cavity, and the mediastinum lies between them. Air in the right pleural cavity separates the layers around the right lung only. The left pleural cavity stays sealed, so the left lung keeps its layers together.
options: Correct. Separate pleural cavities, with the mediastinum between them, limit the problem to one side.
The diaphragm lies below both lungs. Both lungs are in the thoracic cavity, not the abdomen.
A wound through the chest wall is exactly how air enters a pleural cavity. That is what happened to the right lung.
Both lungs are in the ventral body cavity. The dorsal body cavity holds only the brain and spinal cord.

why.correct: The visceral layer of a serous membrane on the outside of an organ is often called its serosa. On the stomach it is the smooth, wet outer covering, part of the peritoneum.
options: The layer lining the abdominal wall is the parietal layer of the peritoneum, not the stomach's serosa.
The fluid is serous fluid, a thin film between the layers.
Correct. The serosa is the visceral layer on the organ's surface.
The muscle layers lie inside the serosa. The serosa is the outermost covering.

why.correct: The diaphragm is a dome of muscle. When it contracts, the dome flattens and moves down, which enlarges the thoracic cavity from below. Air then flows into the lungs.
options: Smaller would need the dome to bulge higher, which happens when the diaphragm relaxes, not when it contracts.
Correct. Flattening the dome enlarges the chest cavity from below.
The chest cavity's size changes with each breath; the diaphragm is its movable floor.
The diaphragm stays a closed wall when it contracts. It changes shape but does not open.

why.correct: Anatomically, the leg is only the segment between the knee and the ankle, the crural region (crus = leg). The thigh, from hip to knee, is the femoral region.
options: That is the everyday meaning. In anatomy the whole limb is the lower limb, and the leg is one segment of it.
The part from the hip to the knee is the thigh, the femoral region.
Correct. Leg means knee to ankle.
The ankle is the tarsal region and the foot is the pedal region. Neither is the leg.

why.correct: Cervical comes from the Latin word for neck, and the cervical region is the neck.
options: Cephalic (kephale = head) refers to the head.
Correct. Cervical means the neck.
Thoracic refers to the chest.
Brachial refers to the arm, from shoulder to elbow.

why.correct: The antecubital region (ante- = in front of, cubitus = elbow) is the front of the elbow. Large veins lie just under the skin there, which is why it is the usual site for drawing blood.
options: Antebrachial is the forearm, from elbow to wrist, not the crease of the elbow itself.
Popliteal is the hollow behind the knee, in the lower limb, not the elbow.
Axillary is the armpit.
Correct. Front of the elbow is antecubital.

why.correct: The upper limb regions include axillary (armpit), brachial (arm), antecubital (front of elbow), antebrachial (forearm), carpal (wrist), palmar and digital. Femoral and crural are lower limb regions.
options: Correct. Brachial is the arm, shoulder to elbow.
Femoral is the thigh, in the lower limb.
Correct. Antebrachial is the forearm.
Correct. Carpal is the wrist.
Crural is the leg, knee to ankle, in the lower limb.
Correct. The axillary region, the armpit, is where the upper limb meets the trunk.

why.correct: The quadrants come from a vertical line along the midsagittal plane, dividing right from left, and a horizontal line along a transverse plane through the navel, dividing upper from lower.
options: Frontal planes divide front from back. They would not make areas you can see on the front of the abdomen.
Correct. Midsagittal plus transverse, crossing at the navel.
Two parasagittal and two transverse planes make the nine abdominopelvic regions, not the four quadrants.
A frontal plane divides front from back, so it cannot mark right and left on the front of the abdomen.

why.correct: Low on the patient's right side, below the transverse line through the navel and to the right of the midline, is the right lower quadrant. It holds the appendix.
options: The left lower quadrant is on the patient's left. The pain is on his right.
The right upper quadrant is above the navel, over most of the liver and the gallbladder. His pain is low.
The left upper quadrant is on the left and above the navel, over the stomach and spleen.
Correct. Low and right: right lower quadrant.

why.correct: The left upper quadrant holds the spleen and most of the stomach. A blow to the lower left side of the chest and upper abdomen often injures the spleen.
options: The appendix is in the right lower quadrant.
Correct. The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant.
The gallbladder lies under the liver, in the right upper quadrant.
The urinary bladder lies low in the middle, in the pelvic cavity, below the quadrants' crossing point.

why.correct: The middle column runs from epigastric (over the stomach), to umbilical (around the navel), to hypogastric (below the stomach, just above the pubic area).
Epigastric (epi- = upon, over; gastr/o = stomach) means over the stomach. It is the upper middle square of the nine-region grid.
options: Hypogastric (hypo- = below) means below the stomach, the lower middle square.
Correct. Epi- over, gastr stomach.
Umbilical is the center square, around the navel.
The left lumbar region is on the left side of the middle row.

why.correct: The top row is right hypochondriac, epigastric and left hypochondriac. The epigastric region sits between the two hypochondriac regions, over the stomach.
options: The umbilical region is the center of the middle row, around the navel.
The hypogastric region is the center of the bottom row.
Correct. Epigastric is the top middle square.
The right lumbar region is the right side of the middle row.

why.correct: Quadrants are named by the patient's own right and left, never the viewer's. Facing the patient, their right upper quadrant is on your left.
options: This step is right. All regional terms assume the anatomical position.
This step is right. The vertical line follows the midsagittal plane.
This step is right. The horizontal line follows a transverse plane through the navel.
This is the wrong step. Right and left always mean the patient's sides.

why.correct: Early on, the swollen appendix stretches, and pain signals from an organ's wall are poorly placed by the brain. They are felt near the midline, around the navel. Later, when the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal layer of the peritoneum on the abdominal wall, the pain becomes sharp and fixed in the right lower quadrant.
options: The appendix stays in the right lower quadrant (right iliac region). Its position does not change; where the pain is felt does.
Correct. Organ-wall pain is vague and felt centrally; pain from the lining of the wall is precise.
The crossing point of the lines is a drawing convention. It has no effect on where pain is felt.
The appendix does not move from side to side. It is attached on the right.

why.correct: The femoral region is the thigh, from the hip to the knee.
options: Crural is the leg, from knee to ankle, on the front.
Correct. Femoral means the thigh.
Sural is the calf, on the back of the leg.
Popliteal is the hollow behind the knee.

why.correct: Cephalic is the head, lumbar is the lower back, and plantar is the sole of the foot. Buccal is the cheek, and brachial is the arm between shoulder and elbow.
options: Correct. Cephalic (kephale = head) is the head.
Correct. Lumbar (lumbus = loin) is the lower back.
Buccal (bucca = cheek) is the cheek. The chin is the mental region.
Correct. Plantar (planta = sole) is the sole of the foot.
Brachial is the arm, shoulder to elbow. The forearm is antebrachial.

why.correct: The nine abdominopelvic regions divide the abdomen into smaller areas than the four quadrants, so they place a finding more exactly.
options: The quadrants are what she wants to improve on. Each covers a quarter of the abdomen.
The body cavities name internal spaces, not areas of the abdominal surface.
Correct. Nine smaller areas give finer location.
The planes are used to draw the grid lines, but they do not name areas on their own.

why.correct: The appendix lies low on the right, in the right iliac region (also called the right inguinal region). In the four-quadrant system that area is part of the right lower quadrant.
options: Correct. Low right corner: right iliac.
The left iliac region is the matching corner on the patient's left.
The hypogastric region is the lower middle square, holding the full bladder and the uterus.
The right hypochondriac region is the upper right square, holding much of the liver.

why.correct: The popliteal region is the hollow behind the knee. Left means the patient's left.
options: Correct. Popliteal is behind the knee.
The armpit is the axillary region.
The front of the elbow is the antecubital region.
The sole of the foot is the plantar region.

why.correct: The right column runs right hypochondriac, right lumbar, right iliac from top to bottom. Directly below the right hypochondriac is the right lumbar region.
options: The umbilical region is the center square, medial to the right lumbar region.
The right iliac region is the bottom of the right column, two squares down.
The epigastric region is medial to the right hypochondriac, not below it.
Correct. Right lumbar is the middle of the right column.
